claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt.
The initial nanoparticles are smaller than 10 nm.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral structure.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at 873 K on a silicon nitride membrane.
Heating equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles from 298 K to 973 K under vacuum activates atomic diffusion sufficiently to overcome high-entropy stabilization.
Surface-energy differences drive Au and Cu toward the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than the other constituent elements.
Au and Cu accumulate at nanoparticle surfaces during heating.
Heating causes an elliptical-to-spherical shape transition.
The elliptical-to-spherical reshaping further accelerates local atomic diffusion.
The proposed segregation and evaporation process is kinetically controlled.
Surface segregation and increased mobility result in evaporation of Au and Cu from the smallest nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles in the 2–4 nm size range will progressively disappear during heating.
The nanoparticle size distribution will widen during heating.
The average nanoparticle size will decrease because of Au and Cu evaporation.
The particles will become more spherical at temperatures notably above approximately 673 K.
The prediction applies primarily to sub-10 nm nanoparticles heated above approximately 673 K.
Initial particle shape, including icosahedral versus truncated-octahedral morphology, can alter the magnitude of segregation and evaporation.
Larger particles or particles heated below approximately 673 K may not exhibit the predicted segregation and evaporation.
High-entropy nanoalloys are theoretically expected to preserve their size and structure at high temperature because of entropy stabilization and sluggish diffusion.
